title: VB9-04304
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Sri Lanka. The Appellant seeks refugee protection in Canada because he fears persecution in Sri Lanka based on his political opinion. The Appellant was attacked and suffered injury in 2005 while setting up venues for political meetings in which his father was a participant. The Appellant submits that the individuals responsible for these attacks were acting on behalf of a political rival of his father. The Appellant submits that his life remains in danger. The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the Appellant has not established his case through sufficient credible evidence. The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in its assessment of the evidence before it. The determinative issue for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is whether the RPD erred in finding that the Appellant has not established a well-founded claim for refugee protection.
I find that the RPD did not err. I find that the Appellant has not adduced sufficient credible evidence to ground his claim for refugee protection.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention1 refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The Appellant alleges in his Basis of Claim (BOC) that, as a young man, he helped his father, who was a member a political party in Sri Lanka - the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX - set up venues for political meetings. The Appellant states that on two occasions in 2005, members of a rival party disrupted preparations for political meetings. The Appellant says he was shot XXXX XXXX XXXX on the last of these occasions.
The Appellant left Sri Lanka in XXXX 2006 to work in Iraq with a contractor providing XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. He returned to Sri Lanka in XXXX 2008 and remained in Sri Lanka until XXXX 2009.
The Appellant went to Dubai in XXXX 2009 and was a legal resident of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) until XXXX 2014.

In XXXX 2014 the Appellant came to Canada on a work permit. When his work permit expired, the Appellant continued to work in Canada without legal status for more than a year from January 2017 until March 2018.
The Appellant filed for refugee protection in March 2018 claiming that he feared persecution in Sri Lanka based on his political opinion.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.2

Sworn testimony at the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) is presumed to be truthful unless the presumption of truthfulness is rebutted. The presumption of truthfulness does not extend to conclusions or assumptions that a witness might advance in testimony.3

I have listened to the recording of the RPD hearing, examined all the evidence and considered the Appellant's arguments on appeal. The RPD found that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the Appellant would face a serious possibility of persecution or that he would, on a balance of probabilities, face a risk to life or of cruel or unusual treatment or punishment if he were to return to Sri Lanka.

I find that the RPD did not err. Based on my independent analysis, I find that the Appellant has not adduced sufficient credible evidence to establish that he faces a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that he faces, on a balance of probabilities, a risk to life or of cruel or unusual treatment or punishment if he were to return to Sri Lanka. Procedural fairness and natural justice were observed by the RPD

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD failed to observe the principles of procedural fairness and natural justice. The Appellant notes that the RPD discusses the Appellant being returned to India in paragraphs 29 and 30 of its decision. The Appellant argues that, while the reference to India rather than Sri Lanka may be a clerical error, the error raises questions as to the attentiveness and awareness of the RPD in arriving at its conclusions and ultimate determination. The Appellant argues that this raises a question as to the level of fairness provided to the appellant by the RPD.

I have conducted my own independent analysis of the record, including listening to the audio recording of the RPD hearing. The RPD Member was fully engaged in the hearing and focussed on the Appellant's claim in the context of Sri Lanka. The RPD Member did not mention India at any time during the hearing. I find nothing in the audio recording to indicate that the RPD Member was in any way confused or uncertain that Sri Lanka was the country of reference for the Appellant's claim. With the exception of paragraphs 29 and 30, the RPD refers to Sri Lanka throughout its decision.

Based on my independent analysis, I find that the two references to India in the RPD decision are clerical errors. I find that the RPD Member was appropriately attentive and aware in considering the Appellant's claim. I find that the RPD observed procedural fairness and natural justice. The Appellant has the burden of proof.

The Appellant argues on appeal that Fernandopulle v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration)4 applies in his appeal. The Appellant cites paragraph 12 wherein Madame Justice Sharlow summarizes an argument put forward in that case that proven past persecution establishes a rebuttable presumption of future persecution. The Federal Court of Appeal found that no such presumption was recognized in Canadian refuge law.

The facts in the present case differ from the facts in Fernandopulle. In Fernandopulle, the IRB found that the refugee claimant had suffered past persecution; the risk of future persecution was the issue before the court. In the present case, the RPD did not find that the Appellant had suffered past persecution on a Convention ground.

In her answer to the certified question before the Court, Madame Justice Sharlow concluded: A person establishes a refugee claim by proving the existence of a well-founded fear of persecution for one of the reasons listed in section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. Proof of past persecution for one of the listed reasons may support a finding of fact that the claimant has a well-founded fear of persecution in the future, but it will not necessarily do so. If, for example, there is evidence that country conditions have changed since the persecution occurred, that evidence must be evaluated to determine whether the fear remains well founded.5
The RPD found that the Appellant has not proven the existence of a well-founded fear of persecution. I find that the RPD did not err. The RPD considered the evidence before it

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD failed to consider the evidence before it. I have conducted my own review of the evidence and I find the RPD did not err for the reasons that follow. Police Reports

The Appellant adduced three police reports in Singhalese with English translations. A clerical error on the part of the Appellant's legal team was corrected at the beginning of the RPD hearing so that the RPD had the correct translations with the correct original reports.6

The police reports adduced in evidence are actually three excerpts from the desk diary of a police station. One of the reports details the Appellant's account of events on XXXX XXXX, 2005 as told to the desk officer at the police station, and one report details the Appellant's account of events on XXXX XXXX, 2005. A third report details the Appellant's father's account of events on XXXX XXXX, 2005. Appellant's account of events on XXXX XXXX, 2005

The Appellant's police report states that "one day two of Mervyn Silva's thugs came to my home and threatened me to stop political activities". The Appellant does not provide details as to when he was threatened or the details of the nature of the threats.

The Appellant's police report states that he was helping to set up a venue for a XXXX political meeting on the night of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, 2005. He states that Mervyn Silva and his security guards arrived at the venue in a black coloured Land Rover Jeep [sic], that they searched for the Appellant and his companions but could not find them because it was dark. The Appellant reported that the Silva group disrupted the preparations for the meeting, shouted threats and fired shots into the air before departing. Appellant's account of events on XXXX XXXX, 2005

The Appellant's report to police given on XXXX XXXX, 2005 states that he was helping to set up a venue for a political meeting on that date when an unknown motorcycle approached the venue at about 4:00 am. The Appellant states that he hid under a stage while the motorcyclist shot randomly. The Appellant states that he noticed that he had been shot in the XXXX XXXX after the motorcyclist left. The Appellant told police that his helpers took him to hospital for treatment.

It is unclear when the Appellant attended the police station on XXXX XXXX, 2005; the time is not noted in the police desk diary extract. The Appellant testified at the RPD hearing that he was in hospital for six days XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.
The Appellant's narrative to the police does not provide any detail as to the identity of the shooter. Appellant's father's account of events on XXXX XXXX, 2005

The Appellant's father's account of events on XXXX XXXX, 2005 details the father's political opposition to Minister Silva and the Minister's alleged corruption. The Appellant's father says that preparations for a XXXX meeting were disrupted by political rivals in a black coloured Land Rover Jeep [sic] that the Appellant's father says "he came to know" belonged to Minister Mervyn Silva. The Appellant's father does not state that he saw Silva that night or how he knew the car was Silva's. The Appellant's father states that the political rivals asked for his son (the Appellant) and that he thought his son's life was in danger. The account provides no reasons as to why the political rivals would specifically target his son or why he thought his son's life was in danger. The Appellant's father states in the report that his son was not an active member of the XXXX beyond helping to set up venues for meetings. Letter from Appellant's mother

The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred by not giving weight to a letter from the Appellant's mother dated April 28, 2019. The Appellant argues that the letter shows that the Appellant faces ongoing risk from Minister Silva and his associates. I have examined the letter and I find that the RPD did not err for the reasons that follow.

In the letter, the Appellant's mother outlines the political activities of her late husband, the Appellant's father, and her husband's opposition to Minister Silva. She states that Minister Silva threatened and harassed her husband but she does not provide any details or dates. Her husband died in XXXX 2016.

The Appellant's mother states in her letter that the Appellant was "injured by gun shot on XXXX XXXX 2005, when he was working to make stage for XXXX program." She does not provide any details on the injury or how it occurred. The Appellant's mother does not provide any evidence of political involvement or activism on the part of the Appellant beyond helping to make the stage in 2005.

The letter from the Appellant's mother concludes, "Mr. Silva and his people need to kill my son. My son have [sic] to work in Iraq in order to protect him from Mr. Silva. Mr. Silva threatening to my husband that he would kill my son. But Mr. Silva still looking [for] my son."

The Appellant's mother provides no details of the threats, dates when the threats were made, or the context wherein the threats were made. She provides no basis for the assertion in the letter that Mr. Silva is still looking for the Appellant.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. (signed) Michael J. Gardiner Michael J.
